artifact.recommendation: Use tail-aware sampling that retains all error traces and requests above the p99 latency threshold, plus a calibrated random sample of normal successful traffic.
reasoning: The prototype exceeded the required 40% cost reduction by reducing stored trace volume 55%, while retaining all injected error and p99 traces.
Errors are rare but highly diagnostic: 0.7% of requests produce 46% of traces used in incident reviews, so uniform or head-based sampling would discard disproportionately valuable evidence.
Tail-based decisions are technically feasible because the backend can apply retention rules after spans are assembled.
Normal traffic dominates volume, so reducing its retention provides the greatest savings with the least impact on incident diagnosis.
Independent, fully aggregated metrics preserve broad service-level latency measurement; sampled normal traces can support detailed latency analysis.
considerations: Set explicit retention rules for every error and very slow request, with a random normal-traffic baseline.
Calibrate normal sampling per service and traffic level so low-volume services retain enough traces for representative analysis.
Preserve sampling metadata and apply statistical weighting when estimating distributions from sampled traces.
Monitor achieved storage reduction, retention-rule accuracy, sampler latency, dropped spans, and service-level sample sufficiency.
assumptions: The prototype's 55% storage reduction is representative of production traffic and cost behavior.
Very slow requests are defined as requests above an appropriate p99 threshold, potentially calculated per service or endpoint.
The backend has enough buffering and processing capacity to assemble traces reliably before sampling decisions.
Full-aggregation metrics satisfy primary service-level latency reporting needs, while traces provide diagnostic detail.
risks: Tail sampling may lose traces when spans arrive late, trace assembly times out, or the sampler is overloaded.
A global p99 threshold could under-retain important slow traces for fast services or over-retain traces for naturally slow services.
Too small a normal sample can bias endpoint-level or low-volume-service analysis.
Retaining all errors may create unpredictable cost spikes during widespread failures.
The prototype may not capture production cardinality, burstiness, or operational overhead.
evidence_needed: Production pilot results showing cost reduction and retention rates across representative services, traffic peaks, and incidents.
Per-service and per-endpoint sample-size analysis for normal-request latency investigations.
Capacity and failure-mode tests for trace assembly, late spans, sampler overload, and buffering.
Cost modeling during elevated error rates and latency incidents.
Validation that p99 thresholds and sampling rules are refreshed and scoped appropriately.

citations.claim: The prototype reduced stored trace volume by 55% while retaining all injected error and p99 test traces.
Errors are 0.7% of requests but account for 46% of traces used during incident reviews.
Requests above the p99 latency threshold represent 1% of volume.
Normal successful traffic represents more than 98% of trace volume.
Metrics are independently collected at full aggregation.
The backend supports retention decisions after spans are assembled.

artifact.recommendation: Use tail-aware sampling: retain 100% of error traces and requests above the p99 latency threshold, plus a low random sample of normal successful traffic. Begin with the prototype policy, which demonstrated a 55% storage reduction, and tune the normal-traffic rate to preserve representative latency analysis while maintaining at least 40% cost reduction.
reasoning: Tail-aware sampling is the only option that directly satisfies the requirement to preserve all errors and very slow requests while selectively reducing dominant normal traffic.
The prototype exceeded the cost-reduction target, reducing stored trace volume by 55% while retaining all injected error and p99 traces.
Errors are rare but highly valuable: 0.7% of requests contributed 46% of traces used during incident reviews, making uniform or head-based dropping especially risky.
Normal successful requests exceed 98% of volume, so sampling them more aggressively concentrates savings where diagnostic value per trace is lower.
Independent, fully aggregated metrics provide the primary basis for service-level latency measurement; a representative random sample of normal traces can support trace-level latency analysis.
The backend supports retention decisions after spans are assembled, making tail-aware classification technically feasible before storage.
considerations: Define error and slowness rules centrally, including status-code, exception, timeout, and service-specific latency criteria.
Use unbiased random sampling within normal traffic and record sampling probabilities so trace-derived estimates can be weighted correctly.
Consider retaining additional high-value categories such as novel errors, unusual routes, selected tenants, or anomalous dependency patterns.
Monitor realized storage reduction, sampler processing delay, memory use, dropped-span behavior, and retained-trace completeness.
Apply per-service or per-route minimum sample floors so low-volume services remain analyzable.
Use full metrics for authoritative SLO calculations and sampled traces for diagnosis and distribution drill-down.
assumptions: Telemetry cost is materially correlated with stored trace volume, so the observed 55% volume reduction is sufficient to achieve at least 40% cost reduction.
The prototype workload and injected tests are reasonably representative of production behavior.
The p99 threshold is available to the sampler and is defined over an appropriate rolling window or supplied through stable service-specific thresholds.
Tail-sampler capacity can handle peak span volume while waiting for trace completion.
The requirement to retain all errors and slow requests refers to traces successfully received and assembled by the telemetry pipeline.
risks: Tail sampling adds buffering, state, latency, and operational complexity; overload or premature decision timeouts could produce incomplete or lost traces.
A single global p99 threshold may misclassify requests across services with different latency profiles.
Aggressive normal sampling may leave insufficient trace-level data for low-volume services, routes, tenants, or regional comparisons.
The prototype proves retention for injected cases but not necessarily every production error type, long-running trace, or partial trace.
A 55% storage reduction may not translate proportionally into a 40% bill reduction if substantial costs are fixed or incurred before sampling.
Retaining every error during a large failure could create a volume and cost spike unless the pipeline is provisioned for it.
evidence_needed: Production cost model separating ingestion, processing, storage, indexing, and fixed charges to verify that the policy achieves at least 40% bill reduction.
Normal-traffic sample rate used by the prototype and retained counts by service, route, region, and traffic volume.
Load and failure testing at peak throughput, including sampler memory, decision latency, trace completeness, and behavior during error storms.
Validation against real production error classes and long-running or partially assembled traces, not only injected tests.
Statistical analysis showing that retained normal traces provide adequate precision for required service-level latency breakdowns.
Operational definition and implementation details for error detection and p99 or very-slow classification.

citations.claim: The prototype reduced stored trace volume by 55% while retaining all injected error and p99 test traces.
Errors comprise only 0.7% of requests but account for 46% of traces used in incident reviews.
Requests above the p99 threshold represent 1% of request volume.
Normal successful traffic accounts for more than 98% of trace volume.
Metrics are independently collected at full aggregation and do not require retaining every trace.
The backend supports retention decisions after span assembly, enabling tail-based sampling before storage.

strengths: The recommendation directly aligns with the stated constraints by retaining errors and p99 traces while reducing the dominant normal-success traffic.
Reasoning is clearly tied to the supplied evidence, especially the prototype’s 55% volume reduction and the disproportionate incident value of rare errors.
The report appropriately distinguishes authoritative full-aggregation metrics from sampled traces used for diagnosis and latency drill-down.
Operational considerations are strong: probability recording, unbiased sampling, minimum service or route floors, completeness monitoring, and centralized classification rules.
The risks and evidence-needed sections correctly qualify the prototype result and identify capacity, error-storm, partial-trace, and cost-model concerns.
Citations accurately map the principal factual claims to the provided evidence.
weaknesses: The initial normal-traffic sampling rate is unspecified, so the recommended policy is not immediately deployable or quantitatively testable.
The report does not define measurable precision requirements for service-level latency analysis or translate them into minimum sample counts.
The rollout guidance lacks explicit acceptance thresholds, staged deployment steps, rollback triggers, and an evaluation period.
It does not reconcile per-service minimum sample floors and additional high-value retention categories with the required cost ceiling.
The confidence score of 0.97 is too high given unresolved cost translation, production representativeness, sampler capacity, and statistical adequacy.
unsupported: The claim that the prototype policy can begin as the implementation baseline is only partially supported because its normal sampling rate, workload mix, peak-load behavior, and cost composition are unknown.
The implication that representative random normal traces will preserve adequate service-level latency analysis is plausible but unsupported without sample-size and error-bound analysis.
The statement that normal traffic has lower diagnostic value per trace is a reasonable inference, but the supplied evidence only directly establishes the high value of error traces.
A stored-volume reduction of 55% does not establish the required 40% telemetry-bill reduction without evidence about ingestion, processing, indexing, network, and fixed costs.
missing: A concrete normal-traffic sampling rate or a formula for selecting one under both cost and precision constraints.
A cost model showing the minimum stored-volume reduction required to reduce the total bill by at least 40%.
Definitions of error, trace completeness, very slow requests, and whether p99 is calculated globally, per service, per route, or over another population and window.
Power or confidence-interval analysis for latency breakdowns across low-volume services, routes, regions, and tenants.
A production rollout plan with shadow evaluation, canarying, dashboards, success criteria, rollback thresholds, and ownership.
Explicit behavior for error storms, sampler overload, traces that finish after decision timeouts, partial traces, and unavailable or stale latency thresholds.
A comparison table quantifying why the two head-sampling alternatives fail the hard retention constraints.
incorrect_assumptions: The assumption that stored trace volume is materially correlated with total telemetry cost is insufficient to conclude that the prototype meets the bill-reduction requirement.
The assumption that injected prototype cases are reasonably representative of production is not established by the evidence and should be treated as an open validation question.
The assumption that a usable p99 threshold is available at tail-decision time may be technically difficult because p99 is population- and window-dependent and can become stale or circular.

Interpreting “retain all errors and slow requests” as only those successfully received and assembled narrows the stated requirement without explicit authorization; pipeline loss may still violate the intended guarantee.
critical_risks: The policy could achieve the storage target but fail the actual 40% bill-reduction target if substantial charges occur before sampling or are fixed.
Tail-sampler overload, incomplete assembly, or timeout decisions could silently violate the hard requirement to retain all error and very-slow traces.
Retaining 100% of errors during a widespread incident could overwhelm buffering or storage precisely when diagnostic telemetry is most valuable.
An undersized normal sample could make service-level latency analysis statistically unreliable, especially for low-volume dimensions.
Incorrect or stale p99 classification could systematically omit genuinely slow traces or retain excessive traffic.
recommended_changes: Replace the 0.97 confidence with a materially lower value until production cost, capacity, and statistical adequacy are validated.
Specify an initial normal sampling rate and calculate projected retained volume and total bill under conservative cost assumptions.
Define quantitative latency-analysis requirements, then derive per-service or per-route sample floors and weighting procedures.
Define error and slowness classification precisely, including threshold scope, rolling window, refresh behavior, long-running traces, and incomplete traces.
Run production shadow sampling and peak/error-storm tests before enforcement, validating real errors, completeness, memory, decision latency, and cost.
Add staged rollout gates: require at least 40% measured bill reduction, 100% retention in an enumerated validation suite, and agreed precision for latency analysis, with rollback on breach.
Model worst-case retention from minimum floors and additional high-value categories so optional rules cannot invalidate the cost target.
Document overload semantics and alert whenever the system cannot honor the all-errors and all-slow-traces requirement.

strengths: The recommendation directly matches the option best aligned with retaining rare, diagnostically valuable errors and slow requests while reducing dominant normal-traffic volume.
The reasoning is traceable to the supplied evidence, with accurate artifact locators and no reliance on external authority or implied consensus.
The report distinguishes broad latency measurement through independently collected metrics from trace-level diagnostic analysis.
It identifies important production concerns, including late spans, assembly timeouts, overload, global-threshold problems, low-volume services, and incident-driven cost spikes.
It appropriately calls for a production pilot, capacity testing, cost modeling, sampling metadata, and service-level sample-sufficiency monitoring.
weaknesses: The normal-traffic sampling rate or calibration method is not specified, so the proposed policy is not yet operational or demonstrably sufficient for latency analysis.

The report treats a 55% reduction in stored trace volume as evidence of equivalent telemetry-cost reduction, although billing may also depend on ingestion, processing, buffering, span assembly, and sampler infrastructure.
The recommendation says to retain all errors and p99 requests, but the prototype only demonstrated retention of injected test traces, not all such production traces.
The stated confidence of 0.97 is too high given the report's own unresolved representativeness, capacity, cost, and sample-size assumptions.
The latency-analysis discussion does not define required precision, time window, endpoint granularity, or minimum sample sizes.
unsupported: The claim that reducing normal-trace retention has the least impact on incident diagnosis is plausible but not established by the supplied evidence beyond the value attributed to error traces.
The claim that sampled normal traces can support detailed latency analysis is not demonstrated without a sampling rate, statistical-power analysis, or validation against unsampled data.
The implied conclusion that the prototype satisfies the cost constraint is unsupported because evidence e4 measures stored volume rather than total telemetry cost.

The suggestion that statistical weighting will preserve distribution estimates is incomplete unless inclusion probabilities are known and the estimator accounts for service-specific and tail-dependent selection.
missing: A quantitative production cost model covering ingestion, tail-sampler compute and memory, buffering, storage, query, and network costs.
An explicit normal-request sampling policy, including per-service floors, adaptive rates, inclusion probabilities, and behavior for low-volume endpoints.
Acceptance criteria for latency-analysis accuracy and sample sufficiency by service, endpoint, time window, and traffic tier.
Rules for classifying errors, including application-level failures, status-code conventions, canceled requests, and traces with missing root spans.
A precise definition and refresh cadence for p99 thresholds, plus handling for new or low-volume services where p99 estimates are unstable.
A policy for degraded sampler operation, including overload behavior, late-span handling, fail-open or fail-closed decisions, and alerts.
Analysis of overlap between error and slow traces and its effect on retained volume and cost.
A cost-control strategy for widespread failures or latency events when retaining every qualifying trace could eliminate the expected savings.
Evidence that trace retention—not another bill component—is large enough for a 55% storage reduction to yield at least a 40% total-cost reduction.
incorrect_assumptions: It assumes stored-trace volume is a reliable proxy for the telemetry bill and therefore for compliance with the 40% cost-reduction requirement.
It assumes injected error and p99 test traces adequately represent production trace-completion and retention behavior.
It assumes the backend's ability to decide after span assembly implies sufficient production capacity and reliable assembly under peak load.

It assumes full-aggregation metrics satisfy the constraint concerning normal-request sampling, although that constraint may specifically require retained normal traces to support service-level latency analysis.
It assumes p99 requests consistently represent every category of 'very slow request'; the intended threshold may require service-, endpoint-, or objective-specific definitions.
critical_risks: Tail-sampler overload, incomplete traces, or late spans could violate the requirement to retain all error and very slow requests precisely during incidents.
Error or latency spikes could cause retained volume and cost to surge, undermining the required cost reduction when the system is least stable.
An undersized or biased normal sample could make low-volume service and endpoint latency analysis unreliable.
If total costs are dominated by pre-sampling ingestion or processing, the policy may meet the storage-volume target while failing the budget target.
Incorrectly scoped or stale p99 thresholds could systematically discard diagnostically important slow traces.
recommended_changes: Lower the report's confidence until production cost, capacity, and statistical-sufficiency tests are complete.
State that the prototype demonstrates a 55% stored-volume reduction, not yet a 40% total-cost reduction, and make final adoption conditional on measured bill impact.

Define a concrete sampling policy: retain all classified errors and threshold-qualified slow traces, then use per-service stratified random sampling with minimum sample floors and recorded inclusion probabilities.
Specify measurable acceptance criteria for error and slow-trace retention, total-cost reduction, sampler loss, and latency-estimation precision.
Define p99 scope and calculation explicitly, preferably by service or endpoint with stable rolling windows and fallback thresholds for sparse traffic.
Add overload and incident-spike controls that preserve high-value traces while maintaining bounded resource use and clearly reporting any retention degradation.
Validate weighted trace estimates against full metrics or temporarily unsampled traffic, especially for low-volume services and endpoint-level analysis.
Run a representative production pilot across traffic peaks and injected failure modes before making the policy permanent.

attacks: The recommendation has not demonstrated the actual constraint: a 55% reduction in stored traces is not evidence of a 40% reduction in the total telemetry bill when ingestion, assembly, indexing, network, compute, and fixed charges may remain.

“Retain all” is presented as achievable, but tail sampling can only classify traces whose relevant spans arrive before the decision deadline; late, missing, or orphaned spans make the guarantee structurally questionable.

The prototype result is weak evidence because injected errors and p99 traces do not reproduce production cardinality, long-running traces, partial traces, burstiness, or overload during real incidents.

The normal-traffic policy is unspecified. Without rates, strata, floors, and sample-size targets, the proposal cannot establish that latency analysis remains statistically useful or that cost stays within budget.

The recommendation equivocates between full metrics and sampled traces: independent metrics may preserve SLO reporting, but they do not necessarily satisfy the explicit requirement that normal-request sampling support service-level latency analysis.

A rolling p99 is not a stable definition of “very slow”: it guarantees retaining roughly 1% even after latency shifts, can normalize a degraded service, and may misclassify sparse services or heterogeneous endpoints.
Per-service floors, extra high-value categories, and 100% incident retention all consume an unmodeled budget and can erase the prototype’s savings.

Retaining every error creates positive feedback during failures: qualifying volume rises precisely when sampler assembly capacity and storage are most stressed, making the hard retention guarantee least credible when most needed.

Recorded inclusion probabilities and weighting do not by themselves repair tail-dependent selection, incomplete traces, or insufficient samples for granular endpoint, region, tenant, and time-window analyses.
The 0.97 recommendation confidence is indefensible while cost compliance, production retention, sampler capacity, threshold semantics, and statistical adequacy are all unresolved.
falsifiers: A production billing breakdown shows that the observed 55% storage reduction yields less than a 40% reduction in total telemetry cost after sampler infrastructure is included.
Peak-load and error-storm tests show any qualifying error or slow trace is lost, incomplete, or decided before its identifying span arrives.
A shadow deployment comparing sampled traces with unsampled ground truth finds materially less than 100% recall for enumerated production error classes or very-slow requests.
Confidence intervals or error bounds for required latency analyses exceed agreed tolerances for any in-scope low-volume service, endpoint, region, tenant, or reporting window.
Applying proposed sample floors and high-value retention rules causes projected or measured cost reduction to fall below 40%.
Service degradation causes the adaptive p99 threshold to rise enough that requests violating latency objectives are no longer classified as very slow.
During representative incidents, retained error and slow volume exceeds buffering, processing, indexing, or storage capacity.
A cost sensitivity analysis shows that plausible error or latency rates eliminate the required savings even when the sampler operates correctly.
Trace-derived weighted latency estimates materially disagree with full metrics or temporary 100% tracing under representative workloads.
The backend’s post-assembly capability fails to provide bounded completion detection for long-running, asynchronous, or partially reported traces.
evidence_gaps: Total-cost model separating pre-sampling ingestion, network, processing, tail-sampler compute and memory, indexing, storage, query, and fixed charges.

Exact prototype policy, including normal sampling rate, workload composition, trace-size distribution, overlap of error and slow categories, and resulting retained bytes rather than trace count alone.
Operational definitions of error, very slow, complete trace, and retained trace, including application errors, cancellations, missing roots, late spans, and partial traces.
Scope, window, refresh cadence, and fallback behavior for p99 thresholds by service, endpoint, route, region, and sparse or newly launched workloads.
Quantitative latency-analysis requirements: dimensions, reporting windows, minimum samples, acceptable confidence intervals, and tolerated estimation error.
Production recall measured against unsampled ground truth for real error classes, slow requests, long traces, and incomplete traces.
Peak, burst, and error-storm capacity results covering memory, decision latency, dropped spans, trace completeness, and recovery behavior.
Explicit degraded-mode semantics and proof that overload handling is compatible with both bounded cost and the all-errors/all-slow retention requirement.
Worst-case and percentile cost projections after service floors, optional high-value categories, and incident-driven retention are applied.
A staged production evaluation with measurable gates for at least 40% bill reduction, qualifying-trace recall, latency precision, sampler loss, and rollback.
Direct comparison showing whether either head-sampling option could be augmented to meet constraints at lower operational cost, rather than treating the option list as exhaustive policy designs.
Evidence that incident-review usage frequency is a valid measure of diagnostic value and that normal or successful traces are not essential controls for causal comparison.

accepted_criticisms: A 55% reduction in stored trace volume does not establish a 40% reduction in the total telemetry bill.
Injected test traces do not establish production recall under late spans, incomplete traces, burstiness, long-running traces, or overload.
The normal-traffic sampling policy lacks concrete rates, strata, sample floors, and statistical acceptance criteria.
Independent full-aggregation metrics do not by themselves prove that sampled normal traces satisfy the explicit latency-analysis requirement.
The definition and scope of “very slow” require validation; a rolling p99 can become unstable or inappropriate across degraded, sparse, or heterogeneous services.
Per-service floors, additional retention categories, and incident-driven retention consume an unmodeled budget.
Retaining all qualifying traces can overload assembly and storage during incidents, when recall matters most.
Inclusion probabilities and weighting cannot correct incomplete traces, tail-dependent selection issues, or insufficient granular samples by themselves.
The original confidence of 0.97 was too high given unresolved cost, capacity, recall, threshold, and statistical-sufficiency questions.
rejected_criticisms: The criticism that tail-aware sampling should not be recommended at all is unsupported by the visible evidence: among the listed options, it remains the only one designed to preferentially retain rare errors and slow requests while sampling dominant normal traffic.
The prototype is not worthless evidence; it supports technical feasibility and stored-volume reduction in its test environment, although it does not prove production compliance.
The backend’s post-assembly capability is relevant evidence of tail-sampling feasibility, even though it does not prove bounded completion or adequate peak-load capacity.
artifact.updated_recommendation: Select tail-aware sampling as the preferred policy, but approve permanent production adoption only after a representative pilot demonstrates at least 40% reduction in total telemetry cost, acceptable recall for explicitly defined error and very-slow traces under peak and failure conditions, and sufficient normal-trace samples for agreed service-level latency analyses. Define per-service or per-endpoint thresholds, stratified normal sampling with floors and recorded inclusion probabilities, overload behavior, and incident-spike cost controls before rollout.
reasons: Tail-aware sampling remains better aligned with the constraints than uniform 10% or head-based 1% sampling because it can prioritize rare, diagnostically valuable traces.
Errors are only 0.7% of requests but account for 46% of traces used during incident reviews, supporting preferential retention.
Normal successful traffic exceeds 98% of volume, making it the principal available target for sampling reductions.
The prototype provides preliminary evidence of feasibility and a 55% stored-volume reduction, but not proof of the required total-bill reduction.
The original report already identified most operational risks, but treated unresolved assumptions too favorably and assigned excessive confidence.
The recommendation therefore remains the same option, while its adoption criteria and confidence must become substantially more conservative.

accepted_criticisms: A 55% reduction in stored trace volume does not demonstrate a 40% reduction in the total telemetry bill; a complete cost model is required.
The prototype does not establish production-grade retention for late, missing, orphaned, partial, long-running, or overload-affected traces.
Injected error and p99 tests are insufficient evidence for production cardinality, burstiness, incident load, and trace-shape diversity.
The normal-traffic policy lacks a sampling rate, strata, minimum sample counts, and quantitative precision targets.
Independent metrics preserve authoritative aggregate latency reporting but do not alone prove that sampled normal traces satisfy the trace-analysis requirement.
A rolling p99 can adapt upward during degradation and behaves poorly for sparse or heterogeneous workloads unless supplemented by stable objective-based thresholds.
Service floors, additional high-value categories, and incident-driven retention must be included in the cost model.
Retaining every error can overload the sampler and backend during failures, when retention matters most.
Inclusion probabilities and weighting cannot correct incomplete traces, tail-dependent selection, or inadequate samples for granular analyses.
The original 0.97 confidence was unjustifiably high given unresolved cost, capacity, recall, classification, and statistical questions.
The recommendation to begin directly with the prototype policy was too strong without a shadow deployment, measurable gates, and rollback criteria.
Interpreting “all errors and slow requests” as only successfully received and assembled traces narrowed the requirement without explicit support.
rejected_criticisms: The concerns do not establish that uniform 10% or head-based 1% sampling is preferable: both inherently lack guaranteed retention of errors and very-slow requests, whereas tail-aware sampling is still the best-aligned option among those provided.

The absence of exact policy parameters prevents production approval, but it does not invalidate tail-aware sampling as the architecture to evaluate; those parameters should be derived from cost and precision constraints.

Incident-review frequency is incomplete evidence of total diagnostic value, but the supplied evidence still supports prioritizing errors because 0.7% of requests account for 46% of traces used in incident reviews.
artifact.updated_recommendation: Select tail-aware sampling as the preferred candidate, but do not deploy the prototype policy directly or claim that it currently satisfies the constraints. First run a production shadow and peak/error-storm evaluation against unsampled ground truth. Define errors, completeness, and very-slow requests using service/route-specific SLO thresholds plus p99 where appropriate; derive normal sampling rates and minimum strata samples from agreed latency-precision targets; and model the full telemetry bill, sampler infrastructure, floors, and worst-case incident retention. Proceed through a canary only if testing demonstrates at least 40% total-bill reduction, complete recall for an enumerated qualifying-trace validation suite, acceptable trace completeness and sampler loss, and agreed latency-analysis precision, with explicit rollback triggers.
reasons: Tail-aware sampling remains the only listed option designed to preferentially retain qualifying traces after span assembly.
The prototype provides encouraging feasibility evidence but proves only injected-case recall and stored-volume reduction under an unspecified workload.
No visible evidence translates stored-volume savings into the required total-bill reduction.
No visible evidence establishes adequate normal-trace sample sizes or error bounds for required latency analyses.
Production recall and capacity remain unresolved for late spans, partial traces, long-running work, and error storms.
The revised recommendation preserves the architectural choice while making deployment conditional on measurable evidence rather than unsupported assumptions.

artifact.decision: Conditionally select tail-aware sampling as the preferred architecture, but do not approve the prototype policy for production deployment or claim that it currently satisfies the constraints.
artifact.action: Run a production shadow evaluation against unsampled ground truth, followed by peak-load, late-span, and error-storm tests. Define error, completeness, and very-slow classifications; derive stratified normal-traffic rates and sample floors from explicit latency-precision requirements; model the complete telemetry bill; and proceed to a rollback-capable canary only if all acceptance gates pass.
reasons: Tail-aware sampling is the only listed option designed to preferentially retain errors and slow requests after trace assembly; uniform 10% and head-based 1% sampling would inherently discard many qualifying traces.
The prototype establishes limited technical feasibility and a 55% reduction in stored trace volume, but it does not establish a 40% reduction in the total telemetry bill.
Injected-test retention does not establish complete production recall under late or missing spans, long-running traces, overload, burstiness, or real incidents.
No normal-traffic rate, sample-size requirement, precision target, or dimensional scope is supplied, so compliance with the latency-analysis constraint remains unproven.
A p99-only definition of very slow traffic can adapt upward during degradation and may be unsuitable across heterogeneous or sparse services.
The revised rebuttals appropriately convert an unsupported deployment recommendation into a gated candidate evaluation and reduce confidence substantially.
evidence: Problem e1 states that errors are 0.7% of requests but account for 46% of traces used during incident reviews, supporting preferential retention.
Problem e3 states that normal successful traffic exceeds 98% of trace volume, making it the principal source of potential reductions.
Problem e4 states only that the prototype reduced stored trace volume by 55% while retaining all injected error and p99 test traces.
Problem e5 confirms independent full-aggregation metrics, which can provide a comparison baseline but do not prove sampled traces meet the explicit trace-analysis requirement.
Problem e6 confirms that the backend can apply retention rules after span assembly, supporting tail-aware feasibility but not production capacity or completeness.
Both rebuttals acknowledge the principal cost, recall, capacity, classification, and statistical-sufficiency gaps; rebuttal-2 supplies the clearest appropriately gated recommendation.
rejected_alternatives: Uniform 10% sampling is rejected because it would retain only a sample of errors and very-slow requests, conflicting with the stated retention requirement.
Head-based 1% sampling is rejected for the same reason and would provide substantially fewer normal traces for latency analysis.
Immediate deployment of the prototype policy is rejected because its normal sampling parameters, total-cost effect, production recall, and overload behavior are unknown.
Rejecting tail-aware sampling outright is unwarranted because the visible evidence supports its feasibility and it remains the best-aligned listed architecture.
minority: The prototype result deserves preliminary evidentiary weight: it demonstrates successful retention of the injected qualifying cases and stored-volume reduction in its test environment.
Independent metrics may reduce the amount of trace data needed for latency work, although they cannot substitute for proving that the required trace-based analysis remains viable.

A production system may reasonably define retention guarantees at the telemetry pipeline boundary, but the problem does not explicitly authorize narrowing 'all' to successfully received and assembled traces.
unresolved: Whether a 55% stored-volume reduction produces at least a 40% reduction in the total telemetry bill after ingestion, network, assembly, indexing, compute, query, fixed, and sampler costs.
Production recall and completeness for every in-scope error and very-slow class, especially with late, missing, orphaned, partial, asynchronous, or long-running traces.
Required dimensions, windows, minimum samples, confidence intervals, and tolerated error for service-level latency analysis.
The normal-traffic sampling rate, stratification, service or route floors, and inclusion-probability scheme.
The operational definition and scope of errors and very-slow requests, including threshold refresh and sparse-service fallbacks.
Peak and incident capacity, degraded-mode semantics, alerting, and the tension between complete qualifying-trace retention and bounded cost.

assumptions: The decision is limited to the three listed architecture options, while implementation parameters may be developed during validation.
The retention requirement is treated as a hard design objective, subject to explicit validation rather than inferred from injected tests.
The prototype workload and stored-volume result are not assumed to represent production billing or production trace behavior.

change_conditions: Approve production adoption if representative testing demonstrates at least 40% total-bill reduction, complete recall across an agreed qualifying-trace validation suite, acceptable completeness and sampler loss under peak and failure conditions, and agreed latency-analysis precision.
Reject or redesign tail-aware sampling if it cannot meet recall because of assembly deadlines, late spans, overload, or backend limitations.
Choose a different or hybrid architecture if head-side classification can provably preserve every qualifying trace with lower total cost and complexity.
Revise the slowness policy if objective-based thresholds, production comparisons, or degradation tests show that rolling p99 classification omits materially important requests.
Block rollout if sample floors or incident retention reduce measured savings below 40%.
next_validation: Build a component-level before-and-after cost model using actual billing data and including sampler infrastructure.
Shadow the sampler against temporarily unsampled production ground truth across representative services and trace shapes.
Test peak throughput, burst recovery, error storms, latency incidents, long-running traces, late spans, missing roots, and partial traces.
Agree on latency-analysis dimensions and precision tolerances, then calculate and validate per-stratum sample requirements.
Define enumerated error classes, completeness semantics, service or route-specific slowness thresholds, stable fallbacks, and threshold refresh behavior.
Run a rollback-capable canary with dashboards and explicit gates for bill reduction, qualifying-trace recall, completeness, sampler loss, decision latency, and statistical precision.

artifact.action: Run a production shadow evaluation against unsampled ground truth, followed by peak-load, late-span, long-trace, and error-storm tests. Define error and very-slow classifications, derive stratified normal-request rates and sample floors from agreed latency-precision targets, model the complete telemetry bill, and proceed to a rollback-enabled canary only if the policy demonstrates at least 40% total-cost reduction, complete recall on an enumerated qualifying-trace validation suite, acceptable completeness and sampler loss, and sufficient normal-trace precision.
reasons: Tail-aware sampling is the only listed option designed to preferentially retain errors and slow requests after observing assembled spans; uniform 10% and head-based 1% sampling would discard qualifying traces without regard to their outcomes.
Errors are rare but disproportionately useful in the supplied incident-review measure, supporting preferential retention.
Normal successful traffic exceeds 98% of trace volume and is therefore the principal available source of volume reduction.
The prototype supports technical feasibility and test-environment stored-volume savings, but it does not prove the required reduction in the total telemetry bill.
The visible evidence does not establish production recall under late, incomplete, long-running, bursty, or overloaded conditions.
No normal-traffic rate, sampling strata, minimum sample counts, precision criteria, or cost reconciliation for sample floors is provided.
A p99-only definition of very slow is insufficiently specified and may adapt upward during degradation or behave poorly across heterogeneous and sparse services.
evidence: Problem e1 states that errors are 0.7% of requests but account for 46% of traces used during incident reviews.
Problem e3 states that normal successful traffic represents more than 98% of trace volume.
Problem e4 states that the prototype reduced stored trace volume by 55% while retaining all injected error and p99 test traces; this is preliminary evidence, not production or total-cost proof.

Problem e5 states that metrics are collected independently at full aggregation, which supports aggregate latency reporting but does not establish adequacy of sampled traces for the explicit trace-analysis requirement.
Problem e6 states that the backend can apply different retention rules after spans are assembled, establishing architectural feasibility for tail-based decisions.
Both rebuttals converge on conditional evaluation of tail-aware sampling and reduce confidence to 0.72 after accepting the central cost, recall, capacity, threshold, and statistical objections.
rejected_alternatives: Uniform 10% sampling is rejected because it has no mechanism to preserve all errors or very-slow requests and would retain only an outcome-blind subset.
Head-based 1% sampling is rejected because decisions occur before downstream error and latency outcomes are known, making it even less compatible with retaining all qualifying traces.

Immediate deployment of the prototype policy is rejected because its normal sampling parameters, production representativeness, total-cost effect, overload behavior, and statistical adequacy are unknown.
Unconditional rejection of tail-aware sampling is rejected because the gaps prevent approval of the current policy, not selection of the best-aligned architecture among the three listed options.
minority: A stricter interpretation of 'all' may make the constraint infeasible for any lossy telemetry pipeline because spans can be missing before the sampler receives them; the guarantee may need an explicitly bounded scope.

If pre-sampling ingestion, assembly, compute, or fixed charges dominate the bill, none of the listed sampling choices may achieve a 40% total-cost reduction without broader telemetry-pipeline changes.
A fixed service- or route-specific SLO threshold may be preferable to rolling p99 for defining very-slow requests, with p99 retained only as a supplemental anomaly rule.
unresolved: The relationship between stored trace volume and the total telemetry bill after sampler infrastructure is included.
Production recall and trace completeness for all intended error and slow-request classes.
Capacity and degraded-mode behavior during peak traffic, error storms, and latency incidents.
The operational definitions of error, complete trace, retained trace, and very slow.
Required dimensions, windows, sample counts, confidence intervals, and tolerated errors for normal-request latency analysis.
Normal sampling rates, strata, floors, inclusion probabilities, and their combined cost.
Handling of late, missing, orphaned, partial, asynchronous, and long-running traces.
Whether the 40% savings requirement must hold during incidents or over a specified billing period.
assumptions: The choice is limited initially to the three listed architectures, while implementation parameters may be added to the selected architecture.
The requirement permits conditional selection of an architecture before final production approval.
The incident-review statistic is relevant evidence of error-trace value but is not a complete measure of diagnostic value.
Independent metrics remain available for authoritative aggregate latency reporting, while retained normal traces must independently meet the stated analysis requirement.
Validation-suite recall can be required to be complete, while real-world guarantees must explicitly state pipeline boundaries and trace-completeness semantics.
change_conditions: Reject tail-aware sampling if a representative cost model or pilot shows less than 40% total telemetry-cost reduction after all infrastructure, floors, and incident-retention costs.
Reject or redesign it if shadow testing finds any unacceptable loss of enumerated qualifying traces, late-span misclassification, or incomplete retention under required operating conditions.
Reject or revise the normal sampling policy if agreed latency-analysis precision cannot be met within the cost budget.
Prefer another architecture or broader pipeline redesign if tail-sampler assembly and buffering costs or failure modes cannot be bounded.
Approve production rollout if shadow and stress tests meet the cost, recall, completeness, capacity, and statistical gates with explicit rollback triggers.
next_validation: Build a component-level cost model covering ingestion, network, assembly, sampler compute and memory, indexing, storage, query, and fixed charges.
Shadow the sampler against temporarily unsampled production ground truth across representative services and traffic periods.
Test peak load, burstiness, widespread errors, latency degradation, late spans, missing roots, partial traces, and long-running or asynchronous work.
Define error classes and service- or route-specific SLO-based slow thresholds, including sparse-service fallbacks and threshold refresh rules.
Specify required latency analyses and derive stratified sample rates and minimum floors using confidence-interval or error-bound targets.
Measure retained bytes as well as trace counts, overlap among retention categories, sampler loss, decision latency, completeness, and recovery behavior.
Canary with dashboards and automatic rollback triggers for cost, qualifying-trace recall, sampler loss, and latency-estimation precision.
